name: Priya Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play alto sax in a seven-piece function band called The Gold Room, which my uncle Rafael books through his events agency. Weddings on Saturdays, company parties on Fridays, the odd anniversary in a golf club. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons I teach saxophone at Hillcrest secondary school, small groups of beginners who mostly want to play the Pink Panther theme. I'm the newest in the band and I still read a lot of my solos off a sheet, which the others tease me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the first dance when the whole room stands up, and the moment a shy Year 8 kid finally gets a clean note. The hard part is the driving, two hours home at one in the morning with the sax in the boot. I still live with my parents, which keeps costs down, and I've got about five months saved towards my own place. I use AI sometimes to write out horn parts for new songs, when the band leader asks for them quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing to worry about, back to work. I'd say it to the band in the van. I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan stays the same. Uncle Rafael's diary is full till next autumn, the school likes me, and I live at home. I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep gigging, keep teaching, keep saving for a flat deposit. Use the AI tool for horn parts a bit more because it saves me an evening. Maybe take grade eight sax so I can stop reading my solos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Uncle Rafael ever retires and nobody runs the agency. As long as my uncle Rafael is booking weddings, The Gold Room plays every Saturday from May to October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close are you to that flat deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two years away if nothing changes. My mother would rather I stayed until I'm married, which is very her. I'd like my own front door before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a wedding needs a real band; you can't dance to a laptop all night. I'd say it to couples at gigs. I'd also say families should support local musicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the company parties are what go. Firms cutting staff won't spend on a seven-piece band at Christmas. Weddings will hold better, because families still save for those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools a bit more, so I can turn songs around fast for the band. I'd ask the school about a third afternoon. And I'd keep saving, maybe push the flat back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, really, but for the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the band if the company parties went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose about a third of the bookings, mostly Fridays. Christmas parties for big firms pay for my uncle Rafael's van, and those firms would be the first to cut a seven-piece band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to Rafael with any ideas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd suggest a smaller four-piece version for cheaper parties. Rafael would grumble but he listens to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to stick together and help each other, and that's what we'd do. I'd say people shouldn't wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the company parties end almost overnight and weddings get smaller. Teaching at Hillcrest might hold for a while, because a kid needs a person to show them where to put their fingers. Robots aren't coming for that till 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard and stay at my parents' longer, forget the flat. I'd ask the school about a full-time music assistant job. I'd help Rafael restructure the band so it's smaller and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The agency is the family business, so if it struggles, it's not just my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Rafael, because the agency is everything to him. My uncle Rafael built the agency from one van and a phone, and I'd hate to see it shrink to nothing in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm welcome at home for as long as I like. My dad would say music was always a risk. He'd be right, but he'd also come to every gig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and families who plan will be fine. I'd tell my students to learn an instrument properly, because that's something nobody can take away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the agency time to change shape. I'd probably keep gigging for three of them. Then teaching becomes my main job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time teaching qualification so I can teach music properly in schools. I'd help Rafael bring in a smaller band. I'd save harder, maybe twenty percent of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. But it feels like something we can work through together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a teaching qualification, rather than just more gigs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because schools need qualified teachers, and gigs depend on people having spare money. A teaching certificate at Hillcrest school is worth more to me in 2031 than a hundred wedding bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still play?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every summer, if Rafael's still booking. I'd never give up the first dance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and sensible people will be ready. I'd say the same to my students' parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can get the flat, get qualified and maybe get married before anything big hits. The band will change, but I'll be a teacher by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep gigging, get the teaching qualification over two years, and buy the flat as planned. I'd use the AI tools for arranging once everyone in the band does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges. Mostly, it feels like normal life with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a Year 8 saxophone pupil today about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That learning an instrument teaches you patience, and patience is useful in any job. A Year 8 kid who sticks with the saxophone for five years has learned something no computer can practise for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any family plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd still want to marry and live near my parents. With ten years of warning, I'd still buy a flat ten minutes from my mother's kitchen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Uncle Rafael's agency would shrink before we could change it, and that hurts the whole family. What would help is more music in schools so there are proper teaching jobs, and apprenticeships for young musicians rather than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. For me, the job and the family are the same thing. Whatever happens to the band happens to all of us.
